The folder holds the full plain-text console.log at detailed verbosity and one binary log per child build. When the build ends, successfully or not, the entry writes a completed marker and copies the log to .artifacts/build/console.log. Each run first prunes old folders. It keeps the ten newest completed folders, deletes folders that contain only a marker, and deletes unmarked folders after 24 hours without a write; a running build writes its detailed log continuously. Retention does not look up the process id that ends a folder name. The test graph targets write test-restore.binlog and test-build.binlog in the run folder. The terminal shows per-step progress, errors, warnings, the Dev Mode preflight lines and the MSBuild summary. --verbose adds the child build output. The file log is always detailed. Directory layout Path Contents Retention .artifacts/bin/<Configuration>/<year>/<TFM>/ Staged product tree of one year Clean .artifacts/bin/<Configuration>/<bucket>/<TFM>/ Compiler output. <bucket> is a year or shared, with an optional flavor suffix; Core builds to <year>-core/, and a tool to <bucket>-tools/<Tool>/<TFM>/, where its copy-local references are hard links Clean .artifacts/obj/ Intermediate output and content-version input lists Clean .artifacts/tests/<Configuration>/<bucket>/<Project>/ Test project output; test.sh build records in .artifacts/tests/ Clean .artifacts/build-tasks/Release/net8.0/ Build task assembly Kept .artifacts/analyzers/<Configuration>/ Repository analyzers Clean .artifacts/assembly-merge/ Assembly merge reference lists and stamps Clean .artifacts/vendor/<Configuration>/handycontrol/net10.0-windows/ HandyControl build output Kept .artifacts/sandbox/<Configuration>/<year>/<TFM>/ Sandbox build output Clean .artifacts/validation-runner/<Configuration>/ Dev Mode policy runner Clean .artifacts/.staging/<build id>/ Candidate distribution in distribution-candidate/Release/, its build.json and validation inputs One root: StageDistributionCandidate deletes the others; PromoteToDist and BuildBundle delete their own .artifacts/dist/Release/<year>/ Published distribution, with promotion-receipt.json in .artifacts/dist/Release/ Kept .artifacts/build.json Build metadata of the published distribution Kept .artifacts/acceptance/tool-contracts.json Tool contract of the published distribution Kept .artifacts/bundle/ Bundle and installer compiler definitions Clean .artifacts/release-assets/ Installer and release files Clean .artifacts/build/ Run logs Ten newest completed runs .artifacts/test-results/ test.sh failed daemon reports, failing TRX files and Design Automation evidence test.sh deletes entries older than 14 days; kept by Clean .artifacts/tmp/ Scratch of the Dev Mode preflight and desloppify.sh Each writer; Clean .artifacts/desloppify-venv/ Desloppify environment Kept Clean deletes every entry of .artifacts/ except the kept ones. It also deletes bin/ and obj/ folders and *_wpftmp.csproj files that a build left in the source tree. It does not enter build/, docs/, vendor/, symbolic links or another Git checkout, such as a worktree under the repository. Directory.Build.props defines the output and object roots. WPF temporary projects (_wpftmp) get a separate intermediate path. The standard target framework is net10.0-windows; Design Automation uses net8.0-windows. Directory.Build.targets adds host warnings, project-reference routing, WPF designer fixes and product and test staging hooks. HandyControl HandyControl is built from the vendor/HandyControl submodule through build/HandyControl/DBTools.HandyControl.csproj. The project imports the four upstream shared .projitems files and the upstream resources, writes transformed intermediate copies that use the DBTools assembly name and versioned pack URIs, and compiles Shared/Themes/Theme.xaml as the theme. The upstream project-root Theme.xaml generated by its PreBuild step is not an input. A missing submodule, resource or transform input fails with its path. Concurrency Run one build or test command per worktree at a time. Concurrent builds need separate BaseArtifactsDir roots; sharing compiler or WPF output between roots is not supported. A nested test command reuses the build-server scope of its parent. build.sh, build.ps1 and test.sh take no lock and do not check free memory. Continuous integration The CI and Documentation workflows run only on manual dispatch, not on pushes or pull requests. CI mode build runs BuildAll; mode build-test also builds and runs the selected tests. The Documentation workflow publishes the site through the wiki server. The release workflow, triggered by a published release, checks that its tag matches Version.props, builds and promotes the distribution and bundle on Linux, then compiles the installer with Inno Setup 6.7.1 on Windows. The self-hosted Windows test runner consumes compiled test artifacts through test.sh and does not build the product. The release workflow defaults to repository contents read permission. compile-installer grants contents write permission for the entire job, including installer compilation and release asset deletion and upload. build-candidate inherits read permission. Both checkouts use the release tag and disable credential persistence. The Claude Code workflow accepts created issue comments and pull request review comments that mention @claude. Classification admits only OWNER, MEMBER and COLLABORATOR comment authors. Bot comments are excluded. The case-insensitive @claude[[:space:]]*review test selects reviews within a line. A review request on a plain issue fails. Other admitted requests use the general job with its write and OIDC permissions. Both model jobs use CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN and claude-opus-4-7. The general job checks out the repository default branch with 50 commits of history, including for fork PR comments. It keeps the checkout credential: the repository is private, and the action fetches from origin before it sets its own token. It disables ordinary hooks with disableAllHooks. Local managed policy files prevent execution, using the same policy-source checks as the review job. For reviews, classification checks out the repository default branch. It reads the pull request API, fetches the numeric pull ref and base commit with full history, checks the head SHA, and prepares the merge-base-to-head diff. The numeric pull ref supports fork branches. No pull request scripts or Git hooks run. The review job has repository and pull request read permissions. It checks the source SHA again and reads the prepared diff and context. Claude runs in native plan mode with only Read, Grep, and Glob. Restricted mode confines file tools to the workspace and prepared-data directory. Read rules deny Git metadata. MCP tools and ordinary customizations are disabled. Local managed policy files prevent review because safe mode and ordinary disableAllHooks settings cannot disable managed hooks. The review and general jobs stop after 60 minutes. Validation requires a successful action, one successful terminal SDK result, the requested init and assistant model identities, usage for that model, native plan mode, the three approved tools, and nonempty final text. Helper models in usage accounting are permitted. Text containing either job credential, known Base64 credential forms, or common token patterns fails validation. Only validated final text crosses to publication in a JSON artifact named for the current run and attempt. Execution logs and token outputs do not cross that boundary. Publication has only pull request write permission, no provider credential, and no source checkout. Issue-comment requests receive one PR conversation comment. Review-comment requests receive one reply in the original review thread. The classified event determines the destination. Returned text remains literal data. Publication errors fail the job. ClaudeCodeWorkflowTests.WorkflowSecuritySuitePasses runs the workflow's inline scripts and classification gate with event, API, policy-file and SDK fixtures. It also checks effective release job permissions and checkout inputs. It requires Python 3, PyYAML, Node.js, and grep. It does not invoke GitHub Actions or authenticate to the provider: ./test.sh test --tool BUILD --scope pure --fixture ClaudeCodeWorkflowTests Source maps and CANON The pre-push hook runs these checks when a pushed path can affect them (Source checks). No build target runs them: python3 .agents/work/canon_source_maps.py writes one MAP.md beside each manifest. A map lists the current source tree, including untracked files that are not ignored, and labels test folders as test mirrors. --check recomputes the maps byte for byte (UTF-8, LF) and fails if one is stale. python3 .agents/work/canon_source_fidelity.py --gate checks folder and namespace agreement, type and file identity, repeated declarations, vocabulary and unresolved rulings for the declared source roots. Troubleshooting Problem Action dotnet or the pinned SDK is missing Run bash build/DotNet/sdk.sh. The .NET 8 runtime for the Design Automation Sentinel is missing Run bash build/DotNet/sdk.sh --test-host-runtime. HandyControl output is missing Run the build from a Git checkout with network access, so the entry can initialize the submodule. WPF designer output collides Build through the repository targets, so _wpftmp gets its own intermediate path. MSBuild task DLLs stay locked A wrapper killed past its exit trap leaves its servers running until the next wrapper invocation stops them. Run the command again. A focused build is slow Build the project or use BuildApp; keep BuildAll for the full distribution. See Architecture Overview, Test Pipeline, Assembly Loading Contract and Sandbox Validator.

developer-guide/architecture/overview.ht.title: Architecture overview | DB Tools
developer-guide/architecture/overview.ht.summary: Architecture overview NAME architecture - the DB Tools assemblies, how they start and how they run a command SYNOPSIS entry DBTools.addin -> DBTools.dll, DBTools.App.Addin.AddinEntry source src/DBTools.{App,Core,Manifest,Presentation,Sandbox}, build/HandyControl tools src/Tools/{Common,Structural,Experimental,Services}/<Tool>/ (manifest.yml, MAP.md source map) years Revit 2026 (2026.5+), 2027: net10.0-windows (build/Distribution/RevitYearContract.cs) placement .agents/canon/CANON.md (where each kind of code belongs) DESCRIPTION Revit loads DBTools.dll through DBTools.addin. Its App code builds the services and the ribbon, and loads the tools from Tools/. Tools from the Experimental folder appear on the DB Tools Testing panel. The daemon (dbtools-daemon) starts Revit for hosted tests. In Dev Mode, it reloads each new build into a running Revit. STRUCTURE flowchart TB Revit[Revit] -->|DBTools.addin| App[DBTools.dll] App --> Core[DBTools.Core.dll] App --> Presentation[DBTools.Presentation.dll] Core --> Presentation Presentation --> Handy[DBTools.HandyControl.dll] App -->|Tools/ path| Tools[Tools/DBTools.Tool.dll] Tools --> Core Tools --> Presentation Project Assembly Role src/DBTools.App DBTools.dll Startup, shutdown, services and ribbon. It embeds every manifest.yml and holds no tool source. src/DBTools.Core DBTools.Core.dll Safe execution, run scopes, call gates, transactions, settings, warnings, logging, banners, and the tool registry and loader. src/DBTools.Manifest Merged into Core The manifest.yml parser (net8.0), shared with the build tasks. src/DBTools.Presentation DBTools.Presentation.dll Themes, controls and window shells, and compiled tool views in Tools/<Tool>/. build/HandyControl DBTools.HandyControl.dll A vendored, renamed copy of HandyControl. src/Tools/<Category>/<Tool> Tools/DBTools.<Tool>.dll One assembly for each tool. src/DBTools.Sandbox Sandbox executable Validates a staged product year and shows the UI without Revit. See Sandbox Validator. Desktop projects target net10.0-windows ($(DBT_RevitTargetFramework)), and $(RevitYear) selects the Revit API references and output folder. Core and SGT also build for net10.0, without WPF or the Revit API, for portable pure tests. The Revit 2026 Design Automation appbundle targets net8.0-windows. CONTRACTS Each rule names its check, if any. References. App references Core and Presentation. Core (net10.0-windows) references Presentation, DBTools.Manifest and the Revit API. Tools reference Core and Presentation. Presentation. Presentation references WPF, HandyControl, HelixToolkit, Serilog, and the Microsoft.Extensions logging and DI abstractions. It never references App, Core, a tool or the Revit API. BuildPolicyBehaviorTests and HelixMergeArtifactContractTests check parts of rules 1 and 2. Sandbox. The Sandbox compiles against Core, Presentation and HandyControl with Private="false", and loads them from the year folder that it validates. No third-party DLLs. build/Merging/AssemblyMerges.props merges each third-party runtime library into the assembly that owns it. The build checks its output against DistributionContract.ProductFiles. Tool assemblies. Tool projects set DBT_IsToolAssembly=true. The build stages them in Tools/ with a content-derived version, which ContentVersionTests checks. One tool folder. ToolAssemblyResolver.LoadAssembly loads only <folder of DBTools.dll>/Tools/<name>.dll, into the load context of DBTools.dll. ToolAssemblyResolverTests checks this. No load context of its own. DB Tools creates no AssemblyLoadContext. Installed, it runs in the default context of Revit. The daemon uses ProductLoadContext for hosted tests and DevModeLoadContext for Dev Mode (Assembly Loading Contract). Themes per view. Each view merges the theme itself and leaves Application.Resources unchanged (Theme System). Fallback log. AppFallbackFailureLog.RecordFailure uses only the BCL, so it works before Core loads. FLOW Startup AddinEntry.OnStartup runs these steps: Idle check (AddinIdle). When DBTOOLS_DAEMON_REVIT_ROLE is set, the copy of DBTools.dll in the default context stays idle. It stores its path in the AppContext data DBToolsDaemon.IdleAddin:DBTools and returns Succeeded, so the daemon can test its own copy. Callback scope. AppStartupBoundary.Start enters ToolWindowCallbackScope, which suppresses ExecutionContext flow and sets contextual reflection to the DBTools.dll context. Start is not inlined, so no other product assembly loads before the idle check. Pending cleanup. AppLifecycleCoordinator.Start returns Failed while an earlier failed start still cleans up. Runtime. Startup reads the Revit year from VersionNumber. AppRuntimeFactory builds logging, services and the tool registrations, and AppRuntimeAccessor publishes them. Preparation. AppStartupPreparationWorkflow runs ValidateTheme, CreateDeferredStartupRunner, ComposeRibbon, PublishInitialStartupEffects and StartBackgroundStartup. The background task installs the main-window owner provider and attaches the hooks. Publication. Startup registers the failed-startup cleanup handler first, then the deferred handlers, and publishes the started state. The deferred handlers apply the deferred StartupContribution effects once the main window exists. A failure in steps 4 to 6 cleans up and returns Failed. A later background-task failure cleans up at the next Idling event. Tool registration ToolModuleCatalog.Discover reads the embedded manifests. For each moduleType, it loads the assembly with ToolAssemblyResolver and creates the ToolModule through its public parameterless constructor. It sorts the modules by order, then by type name. Any error stops startup. AppToolModuleRegistrar stages the settings, services, packs, hooks and ribbon tools of each module, and checks them. A manifest without moduleType adds ribbon tools only, through ToolModuleRibbonRegistrar. ToolRegistry.MergeFrom checks every internal name and lifecycle hook first, and changes nothing on a conflict. A ribbon button names its command by assembly path and class name. Without availabilityType, a command that implements IExternalCommandAvailability is its own availability class. ToolCommand does, and requires an active document by default. Command run ToolCommand.Execute enters ToolWindowCallbackScope and runs through ISafeExecutor. CommandContextFactory.CreateContext calls CommandPreflight.Validate before it opens a run scope. Preflight refuses the command if its panel is off, availability refuses it, or an active warning disables it. IAppRunScopeFactory opens a run scope with the command's profile. InlineUi runs on the Revit UI thread, and QueuedModeless queues work to it from a modeless window. The command returns Succeeded, or Cancelled after a refusal or a failure, so Revit shows no error dialog. See Revit Execution. DATA Item Holds App service provider Logging, settings, hooks, ISafeExecutor, the tool registry and the ribbon state Run scope IRevitRunScope, IRevitCallGate, ITransactionRunner and ITransactionGroupService (RevitServiceCollectionExtensions), opened through IAppRunScopeFactory %APPDATA%\DBTools\ settings.<year>.json, Logs\ and Cache\ (AppPaths) DIAGNOSTICS Logs\DBTools.Fallback.log holds failures from before logging starts, such as a bad Revit year, and failures that the logger cannot record. The log names a failed startup phase, and AppStartupFailurePresenter shows a dialog unless DBT_TEST_RUN_ID is set. TESTS ./test.sh test --tool APP ./test.sh test --tool APP --scope local -y 2026 ./test.sh test --tool CORE ./test.sh test --tool CORE --scope local -y 2026 Selection Covers APP pure Idle check, fallback log, startup effects, failure presenter, ribbon planning APP local AddinEntry, lifecycle, module registration, ribbon CORE pure Discovery, tool loading, safe execution CORE local Registry, preflight SEE ALSO Assembly Loading Contract, Build Pipeline, Test Pipeline, App, Core

developer-guide/architecture/revit-execu.title: Revit Execution and Progress Overlay | DB Tools
developer-guide/architecture/revit-execu.summary: Revit Execution and Progress Overlay DB Tools runs all Revit API work through a call gate, inside a run scope that each command, modeless session or test owns. Tool windows report long operations through the progress overlay. This page owns the design of run scopes, call gates, transaction services and the progress overlay. DBTools.Core describes the rest of the Core library and its source folders. Command entry ToolCommand (src/DBTools.Core/Tools/Commands/ToolCommand.cs) is the base class of every Revit command. Its public Execute runs the command body inside ISafeExecutor and gives the protected RunAsync hook one owning CommandContext; see ToolCommand for the API. Command subclasses resolve services from ICommandContext. Its base interface IAppRunScope exposes the scope's RevitRunScope and Resolve<T>(). A feature that owns a window composes ToolWindowFactory and calls CreateModal for an IModalToolWindowSession with ShowDialog/HideForPick, or CreateModeless for an IModelessToolWindowSession with Show. The session owns the reflection scope and the window's retirement. An expected refusal throws SafeExecutionRefusedException with a reason for the user. SafeExecutor then returns SafeExecutionStatus.Refused, with no failure surface and no exception diagnostics. SafeExecutionRefusalReporter shows a Warning banner, which writes the one Warning log entry; an execution without a banner logs [Refused] {Name}: {Message}. ToolCommand returns Revit Result.Cancelled for a refusal and for a failure. An unexpected exception writes Error diagnostics and shows an Error banner. Run scopes App composition (AppServiceProviderFactory) registers IAppRunScopeFactory with the Core implementation AppRunScopeFactory. CommandContextFactory calls Create(UIApplication, AppRunScopeProfile). The factory selects the call gate for the profile, constructs RevitRunScope, and returns the concrete AppRunScope, which owns scoped service resolution, its IRevitRunScope and disposal. Construction and disposal keep the primary failure, attempt every owned cleanup step and report further cleanup failures in order. Profile Call gate Use InlineUi (default) InlineRevitCallGate Modal commands and daemon-hosted Revit automation that already run on the Revit UI thread. QueuedModeless QueuedRevitCallGate Modeless tool windows and long workflows that must queue Revit API work to the UI thread through the service root's RevitCallGateTask. A tool selects its profile through RunProfile in its manifest; ToolRegistration uses InlineUi when none is given. IRevitRunScope owns the UIApplication, the call gate, document access and disposal. Transaction services are scoped registrations, resolved with Resolve<T>() on IAppRunScope or ICommandContext. public interface IRevitRunScope : IDisposable { UIApplication UIApplication { get; } IRevitCallGate CallGate { get; } UIDocument GetActiveUiDocument(); Document GetActiveDocument(); Document GetVerifiedActiveDocument(Document expectedDocument, string? context = null); } A consumer that keeps its launch document calls GetVerifiedActiveDocument(...). The run scope rejects an invalid expected or active document and requires matching DocumentSessionKey values before it returns the active document. RevitServiceCollectionExtensions registers only the Revit-scoped run-scope access, the call gate and the transaction services. The App composition root registers the Revit task, IAppRunScopeFactory, safe execution, command preflight and the command context services. Revit task Each App service root owns one RevitCallGateTask, the ExternalEvent host that queued gates schedule through. AppServiceProviderFactory registers it as a singleton that is created on first request, with ILogger<RevitCallGateTask>, and registers Func<IRevitCallGateTask>, which returns the task of the same root. Registration creates no ExternalEvent. Startup resolves the task on the Revit main thread after the synchronous preparation steps and passes it to AppLocalRevitTaskLifecycle.Start, which publishes it in RevitCallGateTaskHost. Startup keeps the returned task in its AppStartupOwnership. Shutdown retires and disposes that task before the service root and resets RevitCallGateTaskHost only while it still publishes that task. AppRunScopeFactory, HookHost, ContextualRibbonRuntime and the Foundation Tags update workflow receive the provider. They call it only when they build a QueuedRevitCallGate: a QueuedModeless run scope, a ViewActivated hook attachment or rollback, a contextual ribbon UI call, or the selection actions of an update result. An InlineUi run scope does not resolve the task. A gate keeps the task it was built with. After that generation retires, a new queued call completes canceled and does not reach a replacement task. A provider called after its root is disposed throws ObjectDisposedException. RevitCallGateTaskHost holds the published task for RevitCallGateApiContext, which reads its known application. Call gates do not read it. Call gates IRevitCallGate is the single entry point for Revit API access. It runs synchronous callbacks on the Revit UI thread. Revit API calls outside the call gate can raise invalid-context exceptions or break UI-thread rules. public interface IRevitCallGate { bool InGate { get; } bool RunsInline { get; } Task<T> RunAsync<T>(Func<UIApplication, T> work, CancellationToken ct = default, RevitCallGateMode mode = RevitCallGateMode.Auto); Task RunAsync(Action<UIApplication> work, CancellationToken ct = default, RevitCallGateMode mode = RevitCallGateMode.Auto); } Mode Behavior Auto Run inline when the caller already has a gate context; otherwise queue through the owned ExternalEvent host. ForceQueue Always queue through the owned ExternalEvent, in a later turn. The inline gate rejects it with ContextUnavailableException. InlineRevitCallGate(UIApplication) runs delegates immediately on the Revit UI thread with the supplied application. Modal commands use it. QueuedRevitCallGate(IRevitCallGateTask, ILogger) schedules the callback through the Revit task it receives. RunsInline is true when every accepted callback runs synchronously inside the calling API turn: true for InlineRevitCallGate, false for QueuedRevitCallGate, also while a nested Auto call runs inline. A decorator forwards the value of its inner gate. It grants no API authority and does not describe the current InGate state. SGT's modal session and GM's Commit Review modal session read it instead of the concrete gate type. QueuedRevitCallGate requires a Revit task and an ILogger; RevitCallGateTask requires an ILogger. A missing argument is a construction error. The active UIApplication, the queued-gate depth and the Revit-test depth are internal scoped state. QueuedRevitCallGate owns the queued and test scopes; RevitRunScope owns its application context token. Every scope restores the exact previous value, and a repeated disposal does nothing. Delegate admission Admission is synchronous and runs before the gate validates the API context or schedules anything. Keep asynchronous workflows outside the gate and make in-gate delegates synchronous: await _gate.RunAsync(app => { // Revit API work here (synchronous only) return true; }); Every member of an Action invocation list is checked for an async state machine, so an async void action is rejected. A delegate whose result type is Task, Task<T>, ValueTask or ValueTask<T>, including nullable ValueTask, is rejected. A multicast result delegate with a reference result type is rejected, because ordinary multicast dispatch exposes only the last return value. After invocation, a reference-typed result gets a runtime Task/ValueTask check, which also finds interface-typed Task and boxed ValueTask values. Custom awaiter structs are not detected. Sources: src/DBTools.Core/Revit/Execution/CallGate/{CallGateDelegateValidator,InlineRevitCallGate,QueuedRevitCallGate,RevitCallGateTask,RevitCallGateTaskQueue}.cs. API-context admission RevitCallGateApiContext.IsActive decides whether the current code has Revit API context. Known native entry points use the internal synchronous Enter scope. An untracked call first checks the Revit dispatcher thread, then creates and immediately disposes an unraised ExternalEvent with a stateless no-op handler. Worker threads return false before the probe. Every untracked call probes again. No result is cached across turns. Current exposes a known UIApplication only while the context is active. An ambient application reference does not grant API context. The public UIApplication constructor requires ApplicationServices.Application; there is no public conversion from UIControlledApplication.ControlledApplication. If startup has not received a UIApplication, queued work gets one from the real ExternalEvent callback. No private-field reflection is used. The probe creates a new event instead of adding and removing a handler on a Revit event. It does not change the subscriber collection of the current event and does not write a document, so it is legal in Idling, ViewActivated, DocumentChanged and updater callbacks. Admission does not permit an API that a particular callback forbids; callers must obey read-only and dynamic-update restrictions. The 2026 and 2027 API references list the Create signature and the null-handler exception, but not the outside-context exception. An Autodesk forum thread describes that runtime check and the difference between UI-thread access and API context. The probe does not identify which add-in owns a callback. Inside another add-in's main-thread API callback it returns true, and DB Tools runs inline without its own scope. Callbacks that DB Tools owns enter an explicit synchronous UIApplication scope; later continuations must probe or queue again. The scope is a ref struct, so a caller cannot hold it across an await. Its shared lifetime lets a wrong-thread disposal revoke the context before the misuse is reported. Enter is internal. The build contract suite (RevitCallGateApiContextEntryContractTests) inspects the compiled production assemblies and allows Enter only in ToolCommand.ExecuteCore, the explicit IExternalEventHandler.Execute of RevitCallGateTask, the contextual ribbon SelectionChanged and edit-event callbacks, the ViewActivated dispatcher, the FoundationTags Idling retry tick and InlineRevitCallGate after its own thread and IsActive check. Only Enter constructs the scope. The suite checks call sites in the build; it does not authenticate callers at run time. Global Mapper (GM) has access for synchronous-delegate validation only and does not enter scopes. Queued turns Each native Execute turn of the queued gate runs, in FIFO order, every item that was waiting when the turn started. N waiting calls cost one Revit round trip. Items queued during a turn wait for the next turn. After the first item, a turn starts no new item once its 50 ms budget (RevitCallGateTask.DrainBudget) is used. A failed or canceled item completes its own task; the turn continues with the next item. An item that leaves a transaction open in any document ends the turn. Revit discards what a callback leaves open only when the callback returns, so the next item must run in a later turn. An item that creates a transaction group through RevitTransactionGroups.Begin also ends the turn. Nested Auto calls run inline. ForceQueue defers to a later turn. A caller that needs several reads for one user action makes them in one RunAsync body, or starts independent calls together so that one turn runs them all. A transaction group without an open transaction is not visible to the open-transaction check. Production code therefore creates every TransactionGroup through RevitTransactionGroups.Begin(document, name, validateStart). The factory calls RevitCallGateTurnBoundary.EndAfterCurrentCall(), so the current turn ends when the running call returns, then constructs and starts the group and disposes it if the start fails. The build contract suite (TransactionGroupTurnBoundaryContractTests) inspects the compiled production assemblies and rejects TransactionGroup construction outside that factory. The scheduler posts every raise to the Revit dispatcher at Normal priority, also from the dispatcher thread. A caller never waits on native Raise, a burst of calls shares one raise, and the raise for work left after a turn runs after Execute returns. Denied and TimedOut raise results keep the queue and retry with a backoff from 50 ms, doubling to at most 500 ms, for at most 5 seconds (RevitCallGateRaiseRetry). When that time expires, the waiting batch faults; the scheduler still accepts new work. Each turn feeds a Debug summary with the prefix [CallGate/Turns]: turns and calls, maximum queue depth, the Raise-to-Execute gap, Execute duration, native Raise duration and results, and refused-raise retries. The summary is written when a turn leaves the queue empty, at most once per second, or after 10 s of a queue that stays busy. Turns inside the one-second interval are reported with the next activity. Retirement cancels the posted raise, stops and detaches the retry timer, releases queued delegates and disposes the native event. Dropped tasks never complete, so a worker that waits synchronously on one hangs. Cleanup after a failed startup cancels the tasks instead, because Revit and its callers are still running. Transactions Resolve transaction services from the command scope: context.Resolve<ITransactionRunner>() and context.Resolve<ITransactionGroupService>(). RevitServiceCollectionExtensions registers both as scoped services on the scope's IRevitCallGate. ITransactionRunner public interface ITransactionRunner { Task RunInActiveDocumentAsync(string name, Action<RevitTransactionContext> action, CancellationToken ct = default); Task<T> RunInActiveDocumentAsync<T>(string name, Func<RevitTransactionContext, T> action, CancellationToken ct = default); Task RunInDocumentAsync(Document doc, string name, Action<RevitTransactionContext> action, CancellationToken ct = default); Task<T> RunInDocumentAsync<T>(Document doc, string name, Func<RevitTransactionContext, T> action, CancellationToken ct = default); } Delegates receive RevitTransactionContext, which carries the UIApplication and the Document. TransactionRunner runs on IRevitCallGate and applies the synchronous delegate admission before it enters the gate or starts a transaction. The runtime awaitable check for a reference-typed result runs inside the transaction body, so an awaitable result rolls the transaction back before commit. If doc.IsModifiable (a transaction is already open), it uses a SubTransaction; otherwise it starts a Transaction. It refuses to start a transaction on one document while another document is modifiable. It attaches TransactionFailurePreprocessor, which suppresses non-critical Revit warnings. TransactionRunner enters the call gate and resolves the target document through TransactionBoundary (RunAsync, GetActiveDocument and EnsureNoCrossDocNesting). TransactionExecutor owns the Transaction or SubTransaction lifecycle and names an unnamed transaction DBTools Transaction. The static status validators of TransactionBoundary turn an unexpected start, commit or group-finalization status into TransactionFailureException; TransactionExecutor and TransactionGroupSession call them, and TransactionGroupSession names an unnamed group DBTools Apply Group. await _transactionRunner.RunInActiveDocumentAsync("Create Wall", context => { Wall.Create(context.Document, curve, levelId, false); }); var wallId = await _transactionRunner.RunInActiveDocumentAsync("Create Wall", context => Wall.Create(context.Document, curve, levelId, false).Id); Failure handling TransactionRunner collects failures through transaction or subtransaction disposal before returning a result. The first operation failure stops further work. Existing work/rollback aggregates precede any disposal failure. A single failure keeps its identity, type and original stack. Multiple failures propagate in an ordered aggregate. A disposal failure after commit propagates without undoing the committed write. TransactionFailurePreprocessor.AttachToTransaction sets clear-after-rollback before failure processing starts. Revit holds a stable RevitCallbackRelay (Presentation) that forwards to the preprocessor. After a transaction ends, Revit can keep native copies of the failure handling options until it next pumps, and a Dev Mode reload proves the old generation unreachable before that. Production code therefore declares the preprocessor before its transaction and attaches it with AttachTo after Start, so the transaction is disposed, and rolled back if needed, before Dispose drops the preprocessor from the relay; its records stay readable. For the same reason, copy-paste options get a constant relay (RevitCallbackRelay.Constant) as the duplicate type names handler. Hand Revit a relay, not a reloadable object, for any callback that Revit can keep after the call. A warning is reported as suppressed only after Revit deletes it. A blocking failure, or a fault in a failure accessor, records a blocking diagnostic and requests rollback. An accessor fault keeps the caught exception, which becomes the InnerException of the TransactionFailureException (an AggregateException when several accessors failed). An attachment fault propagates before commit; the preprocessor does not change rollback options inside the failure callback. The preprocessor keeps one TransactionFailureRecord per message it reads: severity, description, failure definition GUID, failing element IDs and whether the message rolled the transaction back. A fault while reading the failing element IDs is added to AccessorFaults and does not change how the message resolves. A runner built with new TransactionRunner(gate, logger) logs every record and every accessor fault at Warning after the commit; the one-argument constructor logs nothing. GM's apply runners use the logging form. TransactionFailureException is the public diagnostic for a transaction that did not reach Committed. Its constructors are internal to Core. Callers read the transaction name, final status, warnings, blocking failure text and failure-definition identities from its properties. BlockingFailureDefinitionIds keeps the IDs in the order Revit reported them, duplicates included, and BlockingFailureDefinitionGuids holds their GUIDs in the same order. The exception implements ITransactionFailureDefinitionSource, which exposes only the GUID list, so code without the Revit API can read it. Core does not classify the GUIDs; GM's GroupEditErrorMatcher matches Revit's four group-edit failures. A posted blocking failure rolls back a runner-managed transaction and raises this exception with the transaction name and the blocking diagnostic. Tool write boundaries map this exception and Revit refusal exceptions to their own typed failures and keep the original exception as the inner cause. Sources: src/DBTools.Core/Revit/Transactions/{TransactionRunner,TransactionExecutor,TransactionBoundary,TransactionFailurePreprocessor}.cs. Transaction groups ITransactionGroupService makes several transactions on the active document one Revit undo entry. It is the manual lifecycle; the caller owns the try/finally around FinalizeAsync, in the workflow that knows whether to commit or roll back. public interface ITransactionGroupService { bool IsActive { get; } Task BeginAsync(string name, CancellationToken ct = default); Task FinalizeAsync(TransactionGroupFinalization finalization, CancellationToken ct = default); Task<bool> IsGroupHealthyAsync(CancellationToken ct = default); } If the document is already modifiable, BeginAsync creates no group, IsActive becomes true, and FinalizeAsync only resets state. FinalizeAsync accepts only TransactionGroupFinalization.Commit (assimilate) and Rollback; another value fails before the inactive-session check. Finalization always clears the active group state and attempts disposal of the owned group. If the operation and the cleanup both fail, the operation failure comes first in an ordered aggregate. Revit rolls back a group that is still open when the API callback that started it returns, and RevitTransactionGroups.Begin ends the queued turn after the current call. Separate BeginAsync and FinalizeAsync calls therefore keep one group only on an InlineUi gate inside one callback, as the modal Super Girt Tool (SGT) and Transfer Drafting Views (TDV) commands use them. Queued modeless work uses IAtomicTransactionGroup.RunAsync(name, work, keep, ct), which TransactionGroupService also implements; GM commit review constructs it directly for its gate. In one gate call it begins the group, runs the work, then assimilates the group when keep(result) is true and rolls it back otherwise. The group is one Revit undo entry also under the queued gate. An exception, or a cancellation seen at any point before finalization (also after the work returns), rolls the group back and propagates. A document that already has an open transaction is refused before any work, because the group would own nothing to roll back. The work must complete inside the callback, where its gate calls run inline. Work still pending when the callback returns is canceled and the group is rolled back. The outcome is classified by the group status Revit reports: only RolledBack counts as discarded and only Committed as kept. Any other status throws TransactionGroupOutcomeUnknownException, and the caller must not report the work as discarded. Progress overlay Hosts Host tool views through ToolWindowFactory.CreateModal or CreateModeless. The typed sessions share the IToolWindowSession lifecycle. The modal and modeless shells expose the WPF owner. Core installs WindowInitializer before the XAML loads and retires its state with the session. Bind an overlay to its window with ProgressOverlay.For(window, logger), on the owner's UI thread. State, dispatcher affinity and diagnostics stay tied to that window. The logger is required. WindowProgressOverlayCapability (WindowProgressOverlayCapability.Hosts.cs) is the only registry from Window to overlay state and visual host. There is no ambient or process-global host. ProgressOverlay.Operations.cs holds the public lifecycle API. ProgressOverlayRunWorkflow.cs owns RunAsync(...): the show policy, the linked cancellation source, cancel observation and hide sequencing. ProgressOverlayDelayedHideScheduler keeps the dispatcher operation it posts and observes every outcome. It clears the pending hide only when the completing operation owns the current cancellation source, so an aborted or faulted stale operation cannot clear a replacement hide. IProgressOverlay Member Behavior Show(title, cancelable) Shows the overlay and resets the cancellation state. Update(status, progress01) Sets status text and progress in [0,1]. A null argument leaves that value unchanged. A non-finite progress value throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException before status or progress changes. Finite values are clamped to [0,1]. UpdateStep(current, total, description, progress01) Sets the status to Step X/Y: {description}. Scope(title, cancelable) Returns a disposable scope. Nested scopes restore the parent state in LIFO order. CancelRequested Thread-safe snapshot of the Cancel button state. RequestCancel() Sets CancelRequested. Hide() Hides the overlay and clears transient state. RunAsync(title, work, cancelable, options, ct) Runs work with an overlay lifecycle and cancellation bridge. A second run on the same window while one is active throws InvalidOperationException. ProgressOverlay marshals public calls to its owner's WPF dispatcher. Do not change overlay state directly from a background thread. Pure and view-model tests can use a simple IProgressOverlay double. Rendering A status change forces a render (RequestRender(force: true)); a progress-only update is throttled. Phase changes stay visible when Revit starves the dispatcher. ProgressOverlayRenderScheduler throttles render requests to one per 30 ms and pumps one dispatcher frame (DispatcherFramePump.TryPumpSingleFrame) with a 20 ms budget and a depth guard. A forced render bypasses the pending-render guard. A pending render older than 250 ms is treated as stuck and replaced. Do not add other dispatcher pump loops or dispatcher-frame code outside that helper while Revit work is active. Cancellation Use RunAsync(...) for long operations. ProgressOverlayRunWorkflow observes CancelRequested, cancels a linked token source and passes the work delegate a token that fires on cancel. After Show(...) resets the cancellation state, the cancel watcher starts before the work begins. SGT analysis (AnalysisSessionWorkflow), SGT placement (PlacementWorkflow) and GM commit review (CommitReviewApplyOverlayWorkflow) use RunAsync. A workflow that drives its own Scope(...) reads CancelRequested and bridges it to its own cancellation. TDV transfer does this: its reporter returns Overlay.CancelRequested as IsCancellationRequested. using (Overlay.Scope("Transferring Drafting Views", cancelable: true)) { result = await _session.ApplySelectionAsync(items, reporter, CancellationToken.None); } Progress values Tools report IProgress<(string message, double? progress01)>: a status message and an optional fraction in [0,1]. MonotonicProgressAdapter (src/DBTools.Core/Progress/Aggregation) wraps such a reporter and forwards non-decreasing values clamped to [0,1]. A null fraction forwards the status and does not change the tracked value. A non-finite fraction throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException and does not change the tracked value. Create one adapter per operation. Tool Progress source Overlay mapping GM MappingPlanExecutor reports per-writer progress (writerIndex / writerCount); MappingApplyState.ReportProgress(message, progress01) reports within a writer. CommitReviewApplyWorkflow wraps the reporter in MonotonicProgressAdapter; CommitReviewApplyOverlayWorkflow updates the overlay. TDV The transfer executor reports per-view stage percentages (0, 10, 25, 35, 60, 85, 100). TdvWindowViewModel.UpdateTransferOverlayProgress maps them through six weighted stages and never decreases. SGT PlacementExecutor.PlaceAsync / UpdateAsync report wall-level and sub-step progress. PlacementWorkflow wraps the overlay in MonotonicProgressAdapter. Record Set ExecutionPlanExecutor.ExecuteAsync takes an Action<int> percentage and an Action<string> log. PlanExecutionWorkflow combines the last percentage with each log message in one overlay update. Common failures Dispatcher errors or missing state: an overlay call on a window that Core WindowInitializer did not initialize, or a change that bypasses the overlay API. Invalid Revit API context: Revit API calls outside IRevitCallGate, or async delegates inside the gate.

developer-guide/architecture/sandbox-val.title: Sandbox Validator | DB Tools
developer-guide/architecture/sandbox-val.summary: Sandbox Validator DBTools.Sandbox validates one staged product year outside a running Revit session. It checks the candidate files, metadata and manifests, then builds the real tool windows and checks themes, layout, bindings and Dispatcher cleanup. It is also a host for developing tool UI with design-time view models. Sandbox is a Windows WPF executable (DBTools.Sandbox.exe, win-x64). Both modes need the matching Revit year installed: Sandbox resolves AdWindows.dll, RevitAPI.dll, RevitAPIUI.dll and UIFramework.dll from the Revit installation directory. Synopsis DBTools.Sandbox [--headless] [--dist-dir DIR] [--revit-reference-dir DIR] Option Description --headless Run the full validation sequence, close every window and exit with the result. Without it, Sandbox opens the window catalog for interactive use. Requires --revit-reference-dir. --dist-dir DIR A year directory (for example .artifacts/dist/Release/2026) or a distribution root that contains year directories. Default: .artifacts/dist/Release of the repository that contains the executable, else of the current directory. --revit-reference-dir DIR A directory with the four Revit reference files for the year. Their metadata must be compatible with the installed runtime. Valid only with --headless. Both --option VALUE and --option=VALUE are accepted. An empty value, an unknown argument or a missing value is an error. Without --headless, Sandbox uses the installed Revit runtime as the reference. A --dist-dir of the form /mnt/<drive>/... is converted to a Windows path. Examples, in PowerShell on Windows after ./build.sh BuildAll. Validate the 2026 candidate against the installed Revit 2026 files: .\.artifacts\sandbox\Release\2026\net10.0-windows\DBTools.Sandbox.exe --headless ` --dist-dir .artifacts\dist\Release\2026 ` --revit-reference-dir 'C:\Program Files\Autodesk\Revit 2026' Open the window catalog for the 2026 candidate: .\.artifacts\sandbox\Release\2026\net10.0-windows\DBTools.Sandbox.exe ` --dist-dir .artifacts\dist\Release\2026 The exit status is 0 when headless validation passes and 1 when it fails. A failure before WPF starts is written to standard error. Process model Each year runs in a new process in the default load context: SandboxEntry uses only BCL types. It parses the options, resolves the year directory and runs SandboxCandidate.Validate. A non-inlined method prepares the Revit runtime resolver and loads HandyControl, Presentation, Core, App and the manifest-declared tools from their candidate paths. A second non-inlined method starts the WPF application. The JIT compiles this call only after the candidate assemblies are loaded, so Core and WPF cannot resolve from anywhere else first. The process exits after validation, so no assembly of one candidate stays loaded for another year. Sandbox creates no load context, does not run App's Revit startup, does not load Revit reference files as product assemblies and does not probe subfolders other than Tools/. Candidate contract A candidate is one year directory of the product tree. SandboxCandidate checks the add-in file, the top-level files, the flat Tools/ directory, the PE simple names, and conflicts with assemblies already loaded in the process. No third-party DLL may be present. Validation sequence Resolve the year directory and the optional Revit reference directory. Check DBTools.addin, the exact top-level files, the recursive Tools/ files, the supported year and framework, and the PE simple names. Read the App, Core, Presentation, HandyControl and tool references and their source-derived versions from PE metadata, without loading Revit API assemblies. Discover the embedded manifests and validate module, command, availability, icon, raw XAML and design-time view model ownership. Load the resources and themes, build the window catalog and each tool window, run layout and interaction checks, capture binding errors, close every window and verify Dispatcher cleanup. Fail if any Revit API assembly is loaded at the end. Portable validation of a distribution archive checks the same file set and also file lengths and SHA-256 hashes. Components Component Responsibility SandboxEntry BCL-only option parsing, year selection, candidate check and the non-inlined WPF start SandboxCandidate Candidate files, direct image loading, PE identity and loaded-image path checks SandboxDistributionContext References to the candidate's App, Core, Presentation, HandyControl and tool assemblies and manifests ManifestValidator Manifest owners, commands, availability types, raw resources and design-time view models AssemblyMetadataInspector PE metadata and reference identities, read from bytes without running Revit code HeadlessValidationWorkflow The headless sequence and its structured result ToolWindowValidator Window construction, layout, interaction, binding errors and cleanup The portable manifest rules are in build/Distribution/Manifest/PortableToolManifestValidator.cs. Tool window registration A tool lists its Sandbox windows in manifest.yml: sandboxWindows: - id: DBTools.MyTool.Main displayName: "My Tool" group: "Common" xamlResource: "DBTools.ToolViews.MyTool.MyToolView.xaml" windowKind: Modal designTimeViewModelType: "DBTools.MyTool.App.DesignTime.MyToolDesignTimeViewModel" designTimeViewModelAssembly: "DBTools.MyTool" designTimeViewModelVisibility: Public windowKind is Modal or Modeless. SandboxCatalog (Core) reads these entries into window specifications, and Sandbox hosts each raw view in the stable Presentation ToolWindowHost. No candidate Window type crosses between assemblies. Validation requires, for each entry: a nonempty id, displayName, group, xamlResource, designTimeViewModelType and designTimeViewModelAssembly; an EmbeddedResource in the owning project with exactly that LogicalName; a root element that derives from FrameworkElement and is not a Window; the host supplies the window shell; no x:Class, x:ClassModifier or x:FieldModifier, no code-behind event attributes, no CLR namespaces of the tool assembly, no implicit templates for tool types, no inferred DataGrid columns and no pack URIs into the tool assembly; a concrete design-time view model whose visibility matches designTimeViewModelVisibility (Public or Internal) and that has a parameterless constructor (public for Public); Sandbox invokes it. Give it fixed display data and no Revit, network or settings services. Design-time view models supply their own unavailable-feature state. Every manifest command type must implement IExternalCommand and every availability type IExternalCommandAvailability, in the declared owner assembly under Tools/. Window checks ToolWindowValidator opens each raw view through ToolWindowHost with its design-time view model and then: measures and arranges the window at a fixed size and at infinite size; selects every tab of each TabControl and restores the original tab; shows the row details of the first three rows of each nonempty DataGrid, except grids whose details are VisibleWhenSelected; records WPF binding errors; closes the window and waits for a bounded ApplicationIdle Dispatcher barrier. It fails when the Dispatcher is missing, shutting down or aborted, or when a cleanup operation is still pending after the barrier. Build output and archives Sandbox is built once per year, although both years use the same framework: .artifacts/sandbox/<Configuration>/<year>/<TFM>/ build output sandbox/<year>/<sanitized-tfm>/ path inside the validation archive ./build.sh PackageSandboxValidationInput writes a content-addressed validate-dist-<sha256>.zip with the candidate and Sandbox. The DIST suite consumes that archive and writes a structured result JSON (see Distribution acceptance). The archive and the result keep normalized relative paths. The portable validation of the archive runs on any host and checks files and metadata only. The Windows acceptance suite runs DBTools.Sandbox.exe --headless for each year, with the reference files the archive carries under revit-refs/<year>/, so the window checks run there. Troubleshooting Failure Where to look Candidate file missing or extra ProductOutput staging and DistributionContract .addin entry mismatch build/Installer/DBTools.addin and the App output Tool assembly missing The manifest assembly name and Tools/ staging Raw XAML resource missing EmbeddedResource LogicalName in the owning project Design-time view model cannot be created Its visibility, designTimeViewModelVisibility and parameterless constructor Binding errors Explicit bindings and the stable Presentation templates Layout failure ToolWindowValidator measure and arrange messages Cleanup timeout Dispatcher and window owner lifetime A window failure reports both the primary exception and any cleanup exception. See Sandbox Integration, Assembly Loading Contract and Test Pipeline.

developer-guide/architecture/structural-.title: Structural Preview | DB Tools
developer-guide/architecture/structural-.summary: Structural Preview DBTools.Presentation.StructuralPreview is the stable WPF host for the structural 3D preview shared by the Extreme Roof Framing Tool (ERFT) and the Super Girt Tool (SGT). A tool adapter supplies immutable scene data and receives pointer events. The host owns the Helix viewport, effects manager, camera, navigation, materials, hit testing, tooltip, overlay markers and cleanup. Helix and SharpDX are merged into Presentation as internal types; no tool assembly or raw view names them. ERFT and SGT register the presenter's disposal with their tool-window sessions. The component has no Core, App or tool-assembly dependency. Its public scene records contain only immutable arrays, System.Numerics values, strings, integers and scalar values. Attach and dispose Call StructuralPreview3DFactory.Attach on the viewport host dispatcher. The ContentControl must be empty. The optional overlay canvas must use the same dispatcher. The returned IStructuralPreview3D owns one viewport and one effects manager. All presenter methods and disposal are synchronous UI-thread operations. Attach returns a disabled presenter with the load error as its reason when Helix libraries cannot be loaded. The disabled presenter still validates and copies supplied scene and emphasis data, reports its status reason, returns false from projection, and can be disposed repeatedly. For an available presenter, Dispose removes viewport, camera, owner-window, timer and input handlers; closes the tooltip; removes only the overlay children created by this presenter; disposes owned scene elements, viewport and effects manager; clears scene data and subscriber events; and clears the host content only when that content is still the viewport owned by this presenter. Cleanup is synchronous and does not post a dispatcher frame. Disposal clears subscriptions before cleanup, so it publishes zero presenter events during or after disposal. Repeated disposal is safe. Scene data and picks SetScene validates and deep-copies the supplied records and arrays. The caller may then release or reuse its own objects. Equal mesh geometry keeps existing Helix models; geometry or appearance changes update the rendered decorations and materials, while bounds or exterior-normal changes update camera state. Mesh Opacity supplies the material alpha and overrides the alpha byte in Argb. Line sets multiply their ARGB alpha by Opacity. Selection and hover colors preserve the mesh opacity. Mesh picking is independent of emphasis. A mesh is eligible for a hit only when its supplied IsPickable value is true; context meshes can therefore be pickable or non-pickable independently of their material role. A floor is supplied as scene geometry, normally a context mesh with IsPickable: false. Line sets and non-pickable meshes do not produce mesh hits. A missed hit has null mesh ID, null context ID and null world point. A hit's mesh and context hits are resolved independently: each is the nearest eligible hit for its role. MeshId is the nearest member ID, or null when there is no member hit; ContextId is the nearest context ID independently. WorldPoint is the nearest member hit point when one exists, otherwise the context hit point, so a context-only hit has a null mesh ID and a context world point. The event also carries WPF screen coordinates relative to the viewport and keyboard modifiers. SetEmphasis accepts one emphasis state per mesh ID. The presenter applies selection, segment-selection, sibling, dimmed and hover material policies from the selected StructuralPreviewPalette. StructuralPreviewPalette.Sgt and .Erft are the adapter presets. They differ in member color boost, surfaces, selection and hover colors, and edge and outline settings, and use the same renderer. The presenter adds a pivot marker to the supplied overlay canvas while orbiting. The marker and all generated WPF objects have their data context cleared or blocked so tool data contexts do not flow into the stable visual tree. Home views and camera movement The ExteriorThreeQuarter strategy is the SGT home view. When bounds or the exterior normal changes, the session recomputes and stores a raw Home camera. Its exact formula is: distance = max(2.2 * boundsDiagonal, 8) yaw = 28 degrees pitch = 0.22 downward along the configured up axis The exterior normal is projected onto the up plane. A missing horizontal normal uses negative Y as the stable fallback. The stored Home keeps this exact distance. Clamping applies to the displayed camera only. If the user has moved the camera, a changed scene clamps the current camera and retains the new raw Home for a later reset. Reset clears the moved flag, applies Home, and clamps the displayed camera. ERFT uses the PreserveAngle strategy. When bounds change, the session fits the current view angle and captures that result as Home. The fit formula is: halfV = radians(fieldOfView) / 2 halfH = atan(tan(halfV) * aspect) distance = max(boundsDiagonal / 2 / sin(min(halfV, halfH)), 2) * 1.2 Helix FieldOfView is the vertical angle. The fit keeps the bounds' bounding sphere inside both the vertical and the horizontal field of view, so the whole scene is visible at the viewport aspect when the fit runs; the distance clamp still applies. Scene constraints use these bounds-only constants (StructuralPreviewCameraMath): diagonal = actualDiagonal, or 10 when actualDiagonal <= 1e-6 min = clamp(diagonal * 0.0005, 0.005, 0.75) max = clamp(diagonal * 40, min * 2, 50000) targetPad = max(2, diagonal * 6) near = max(0.0005, min * 0.05) far = max(100, max * 2) When a scene changes mesh geometry without changing these bounds, the presenter keeps the stored Home object and only updates its owned render models. Adapters must compute bounds from every mesh vertex so a real extent change is reported as a bounds change; a bounds change is an intentional Home refit under PreserveAngle. ZoomToFit performs the exact fit. When FitRedefinesHome is enabled, the fitted camera becomes Home and the viewport default camera is updated to the same pose; otherwise the fit marks the camera as user-moved while preserving Home. ResetView restores stored Home. Pan uses screen-space camera axes, orbit uses the configured arbitrary up axis around the selected or picked pivot, and wheel zoom moves toward the picked world anchor. Gesture cancellation occurs on lost capture, window deactivation, unload and disabled interaction. The viewport's native view cube handles its own preview input before scene picking. The presenter keeps the default camera synchronized with stored scene Home when a scene is attached; an explicit fit also updates it when FitRedefinesHome is enabled. Input and hover StructuralPreview3DOptions.ShowTooltips defaults to true. It enables the stable presenter's mesh tooltips. When disabled, pointer updates keep the tooltip closed. Materials and lighting Adapters choose StructuralPreviewPalette.Sgt or .Erft and can copy the record to adjust individual values. A palette supplies member and context surfaces, key/fill/rim/ambient light colors, sibling and dimmed policies, selection and hover colors, emissive scaling, edge colors and thickness, outline mode and pivot colors. IsPickable controls hit testing. A non-pickable context mesh remains rendered with its base context material but bypasses selection, segment-selection, sibling, dimmed and hover emphasis; pickable context meshes can receive context hover, sibling and dimmed states but never member selection states. The SGT preset uses these alpha rules. Sibling emphasis scales diffuse alpha by 0.70 and retains the source ambient, specular and emissive alpha. Dimmed emphasis sets every channel's alpha to max(0.05, sourceAlpha * 0.45). Hovering a sibling restores the base material and adds emissive brightness while preserving its source alpha. Hovering a dimmed mesh adds emissive brightness and retains the dimmed alpha. The default options select the SGT palette and exterior home strategy. ERFT selects both its palette and its camera strategy: var options = new StructuralPreview3DOptions { Palette = StructuralPreviewPalette.Erft, HomeView = StructuralPreviewHomeView.PreserveAngle }; Diagnostics and projection Diagnostic reports debug, warning and error messages as plain strings with an optional exception. Repeated identical diagnostic messages are suppressed for two seconds. An initialization or disabled-path diagnostic is delivered once to the first diagnostic subscriber; the reason is also available in Status. Event publication takes an invocation-list snapshot and stops when a callback disposes the presenter. No presenter event is raised after Dispose clears subscriptions. On the first render failure, the presenter changes to Unavailable, disables interaction, cancels navigation, clears hover state, stops its clamp timer and collapses the viewport. It reports that failure as an error diagnostic, subject to the two-second diagnostic de-duplication; later render failures are ignored while the presenter is unavailable. TryProjectToViewport returns false when the presenter is unavailable, disposed, unloaded, has no render context, receives a non-finite point, has an invalid camera or the point is behind the camera. It returns WPF device- independent coordinates relative to the viewport on success. Projection failures are reported as debug diagnostics and never escape as exceptions. Public API The following declarations are the public API. Rendering records are in DBTools.Presentation.StructuralPreview.Rendering; configuration and events are in DBTools.Presentation.StructuralPreview. public static class StructuralPreview3DFactory { public static IStructuralPreview3D Attach( ContentControl viewportHost, Canvas? overlay, StructuralPreview3DOptions options); } public interface IStructuralPreview3D : IDisposable { bool IsAvailable { get; } StructuralPreview3DStatus Status { get; } event EventHandler? developer-guide/architecture/test-pipeli.title: Test Pipeline | DB Tools
developer-guide/architecture/test-pipeli.summary: Test Pipeline This page describes how DB Tools tests are selected, staged and run. For the test.sh options, examples and the rules for writing tests, see Testing Tools. DB Tools tests run through one of two routes: ./test.sh resolves the selected projects, builds them, freezes their inputs and runs them locally or submits them to the dbtools-daemon fleet. It writes the receipts that --no-build and CI consume. See the test.sh command reference. Plain dotnet test on an entry project in testing/Daemon/ uses the pinned daemon VSTest adapter (DbToolsDaemon.RevitTest.TestAdapter). MSBuild builds the selected assemblies, models, includes and per-year sources, and the adapter submits them in one request. See Daemon adapter entry projects. Use one route per invocation. Both read the relay URL from DBTOOLS_DAEMON_RELAY_URL; the daemon owns relay credentials, and neither route accepts or stores them. Scopes and suites Scope or suite Marker Where it runs Pure tests (pure) plain [Test] Without Revit. Locally when possible; otherwise as a daemon PureSuite job on a hidden Windows desktop Revit-hosted tests (local) [RevitLocal] Inside Revit on a daemon worker, for one selected year Design Automation tests (da) [RevitDA] On the invoking host as a budgeted APS client; external run records feed Studio DIST The Windows distribution acceptance suite, always a daemon PureSuite job BUILD Linux-native build and distribution contract suites Revit-hosted tests exercise the real ribbon, WPF and add-in lifecycle in Revit. The scheduled runner builds the Revit 2026 Sentinel test project and submits one capped WorkItem. Offline Sentinel tests use the Pure scope. See APS Design Automation Sentinel. Pure requests have no year. A Revit-hosted request for two years makes one daemon request per year, each with its own product tree and report. Design Automation tests always build Revit 2026. Selection test.sh list --projects prints the sorted scope<TAB>project rows and is the source of truth for what a request selects. It evaluates project membership, explicit Compile Include, Exclude and Remove items, disabled default items, NUnit fixture attributes and the selected tool, scope and year. The same index resolves fixtures and exact FQNs. A fixture must resolve to one compiled owner class. An unknown fixture or project, an unreadable project or source file, a project the selected tool and scope cannot reach, or an explicit scope with no resolved project exits with status 2 before any build or submission. An exact FullyQualifiedName=<FQN> filter becomes an exact daemon selector, and a prefix filter becomes a prefix selector. A Revit-hosted filter that cannot be mapped exits with status 2 instead of selecting the whole assembly. Pure routing test.sh checks each selected Pure assembly for its .deps.json, .runtimeconfig.json and the output-local NUnit3.TestAdapter.dll, then routes it: to the daemon if it is the DIST suite or a machine is pinned; to the daemon if it targets Windows and the host is not Windows; to the daemon if the host lacks Microsoft.WindowsDesktop.App; a missing other framework is an error; otherwise to local VSTest. Projects that run locally, including the Linux BUILD and Distribution suites, run one after another; daemon submissions run concurrently, at most DBT_PURE_CONCURRENCY (default 2) at a time. A local project that runs zero tests fails. With a filter expression, the run fails only when no selected project runs a test. Linux-native BUILD projects and *.Portable.Pure.Tests projects are skipped on Windows with a notice. User interface input By default, a daemon job, Pure or Revit-hosted, runs on the daemon's private desktop, which receives no keyboard or mouse input and never becomes the foreground, whether the Windows session is locked or not. Tests drive the user interface in-process: through view-model commands, WPF automation peer providers, RaiseEvent, Keyboard.Focus or FocusManager in the test's own windows, and the calling thread's own Win32 state (SetActiveWindow, SetKeyboardState, messages to its own windows); or through UI Automation patterns in another process. A test project fails to build when it uses an API listed in testing/BannedSymbols.txt (error RS0030) or when its source names an OS input or foreground function such as SendInput or SetForegroundWindow (error DBT0003, DBT_RejectOsInputInterop in Directory.Build.targets). Inputs and receipts For a selected scope and year, the MSBuild graph returns the test assembly, target framework, model items and product-tree includes in one pass. Before any submission, test.sh freezes the assemblies, runtime closure, product-tree includes, models and companions into the content-addressed test input cache (DBT_TEST_INPUT_CACHE_ROOT), so a later build cannot change the submitted files. A normal exit removes the per-run directory. The default cache is $TMPDIR/dbtools-test-inputs/<repository hash>; with it, each test and submit deletes the caches of other repositories in that folder that no run used for 7 days. --compile-only writes a receipt bound to the source identity, the selected projects, the graph inputs and the output hashes. --no-build verifies all of these and refuses stale or missing files. CI resolves the selectors once with ./test.sh list --projects, compiles each selected scope with --compile-only, transfers the receipt and the recorded input closure, and runs them with --no-build. The consumer never rebuilds. Linux BUILD and DIST jobs do not depend on the Windows transfer. The portable BUILD project selection requires no prebuilt product or candidate output: ./test.sh test --tool BUILD --project testing/DBTools.Build.Tests/DBTools.Build.Tests.csproj --scope pure --filter 'TestCategory!=ProductArtifacts' --tool BUILD also selects the Distribution and Sandbox projects. Their setup requirements remain separate. Ordinary test compilation creates test artifacts under .artifacts. The complete --filter 'TestCategory=ProductArtifacts' selection requires a source-current ./build.sh BuildAll and compiled hosted test outputs. It checks promoted distributions, compiler PDBs, merge inputs and hosted test outputs. AssembleDistributionCandidate alone does not supply all of these inputs. Artifact admission inspects every staged build.json and the final record. It selects the newest parsed builtAtUtc whose sourceCommit and sourceTree match HEAD and its tree. Admission requires clean tracked and untracked source, including root build configuration and documentation. Distributed bytes must match the declared distributionFingerprint before tests read them. Compiler PDBs, merge inputs and dependency files require current BuildAll outputs as setup; the distribution fingerprint does not authenticate those intermediate files. The Presentation ToolWindowXamlTests fixture, compiled by Presentation Pure, parses raw XAML from every tool in DistributionContract.ToolAssemblyFiles and Core. Its project references supply the complete tool set to the test consumer. Results Daemon summary and full-report JSON require a command envelope with the report under result.report. A document without the envelope fails validation. After a zero submit exit, the summary must report result_status=passed, a positive passed count, and zero failed, errored, and aborted counts. Skipped tests can accompany passed tests. Zero executed tests, including an all-skipped run, fail admission. A nonzero submit exit is kept even when the terminal JSON is missing or malformed. When retrieval succeeds, failed runs keep their reports and original exit status. A refused submit (ok: false, a null result and an error) ran nothing: the wrapper prints the error code, summary, causes and next step, fetches no report, and keeps the CLI's nonzero exit, or returns 2 after a zero exit. Other rejected terminal summaries are saved as *.invalid-summary.json. Full report retrieval accepts a report exit of zero or the submit exit. The report file must be nonempty, and its JSON request identity, status, and counts must match the accepted summary. Retrieval makes three report attempts, stopping after the first accepted report. Two one-second delays separate three failed attempts. It never resubmits tests. Only an accepted report is published to the result path. After exhaustion, nonempty rejected output is saved as PATH.invalid-report.json, where PATH is the full report path. A refused report command prints its error code, summary, causes and next step whatever its exit; only a refusal with exit 3 is fetched again, and a refused report is not saved. The wrapper keeps a nonzero submit exit or returns 2 after a zero submit exit. Independent scopes in one request continue after a failure, but test.sh returns the first nonzero status. Daemon adapter entry projects testing/Daemon/Hosted/<Tool>.Hosted.Entry.csproj builds DBTools.<Tool>.Local.Tests for both years (Hosted2026.proj, Hosted2027.proj). <Tool> is a tool key or App, Core or Presentation. The App and Core entries also build DBTools.<Tool>.HostedTurns.Local.Tests. testing/Daemon/Pure/<Tool>.Pure.Entry.csproj selects every DBTools.<Tool>.*Pure.Tests.csproj beside its owner. After the build, the entry writes dbtools-daemon.runsettings from Hosted.runsettings or Pure.runsettings with the literal sources, models and includes. The hosted settings default to years 2026,2027, isolated execution and a 30-minute timeout, and treat a run with no tests as an error. Product staging Each Revit-hosted test for a year receives the product tree that the installer uses, under product/<year>/. The tree keeps its relative paths. Test assemblies and NUnit and adapter dependencies are separate inputs. App loads tools from Tools/ by explicit path into the context that holds it, so ProductLoadContext and DevModeLoadContext receive the same identities as the staged tree. Test support installs no resolver for product assemblies. Test projects Test projects are next to their production owners: src/DBTools.App/Tests/DBTools.App.{Pure,Local}.Tests.csproj src/DBTools.Core/Tests/DBTools.Core.{Pure,Local}.Tests.csproj src/DBTools.Presentation/Tests/DBTools.Presentation.{Pure,Local}.Tests.csproj src/DBTools.Sandbox/Tests/DBTools.Sandbox.Pure.Tests.csproj src/Tools/<Category>/<Tool>/Tests/DBTools.<Tool>.{Pure,Local}.Tests.csproj testing/DBTools.Build.Tests/ build and distribution contracts (Linux) testing/DBTools.Distribution.Tests/ portable archive contracts, Dev Mode unload (Linux) testing/DBTools.Distribution.Windows.Tests/ DIST suite testing/RevitTestModels/ test models by year and tool An owner has both a .Pure.Tests and a .Local.Tests project only when both kinds of test exist. Pure projects list their source files explicitly and reference their normal production owners. Shared props give every Pure project $(DBT_PureRevitYear) (2026) and static graph restore, and pass that year on owner references, so a plain dotnet build or dotnet test of one project needs no properties. Revit is compile-only in Pure tests: a test must not load Revit-typed members or scan owner types outside the loadable set. .Local.Tests projects disable default compile items and include only Revit-hosted fixtures. Presentation tests are under Presentation and belong to the Presentation projects, also when they test a tool's Presentation types. Presentation Pure links the Core test support it shares and references Core for the tool window, window runtime and logger window integration fixtures. Tests that need a real WPF window run where Windows is available. Portable Pure projects Core and the Super Girt Tool (SGT) define an optional $(DBT_PortableTargetFramework). Their *.Portable.Pure.Tests projects build against that framework and run on Linux; CI and Windows test.sh route them to Linux. To make a project portable: declare desktop and portable TargetFrameworks; condition DBT_RevitHostIdentity, UseWPF and the Presentation ProjectReference on the desktop framework, and keep Revit references under the desktop host identity condition; set DBT_UsesMergedAssemblies=false in portable consumers. build/MSBuild/Portable.targets excludes App, Revit, Views, DesignTime and XAML inputs. Portable images use ordinary NuGet dependencies, have no content version and add no staged runtime files. Core uses an explicit list of source files for its portable build. Test models Revit-hosted projects declare RevitTestModel items relative to testing/RevitTestModels: testing/RevitTestModels/ ├── 2026/GM/gm_test_model.rvt ├── 2026/SGT/sgt_test_model.rvt ├── 2026/SGT/_LinkedModels/sgt_test_linked_model.rvt ├── 2026/Regression/realtest_model.rvt ├── 2027/... (same layout) ├── GM/SharedParameters/shared_parameters.txt └── VTC/vtc_import_layers.dxf Model files and explicit non-RVT inputs keep their relative paths in the daemon stage. Revit-hosted fixtures find them under DBTOOLS_DAEMON_REVIT_MODELS_DIR; Pure fixtures use the repository root in DBT_TEST_REPO_ROOT. TestPathResolver reads the root on every call, so a job never sees the model root of a previous job. A fixture may open a temporary copy of a model, but the daemon owns the active document and the worker lifecycle. Models resolve only from these roots, not from a worker checkout or an %APPDATA% cache. Test support testing/TestSupport holds shared test infrastructure and doubles for true externals. Tool-specific doubles are under testing/TestSupport/<Tool> and are linked as source by the matching test projects; they are not a separate assembly. Revit/RevitHost.cs initializes the year, the App runtime and the product Revit call gate before the test body, and supplies the real UIApplication through an ambient scope that does not carry API access across an await. It owns the scheduler unless a fixture holds a longer lease. A test that builds a QueuedRevitCallGate passes the fixture's Revit task; a borrowed task stays with its publisher. A QueuedModeless run scope from the App runtime schedules through that runtime's own task. Forced-queue tests call the real external-event handler synchronously to model a later API turn; one daemon NUnit callback contains no second native turn. Wpf/WpfTestRuntimeBootstrap.cs registers pack URI support, installs the shared window owner, validates themes in the runtime assembly's contextual reflection scope, and releases only its own provider at teardown. It adds no Resolving handlers and does not force Presentation or HandyControl into the default context. Logging/TestLoggingBridge.cs uses production logging when Revit provides it and a console and file host otherwise. Revit-hosted fixtures release only their own runtime, Revit task, owner handle and window resources. Cleanup reports both the primary failure and any cleanup failure. See Build Pipeline, Assembly Loading Contract and Sandbox Validator.

developer-guide/architecture/theme-syste.title: Theme System | DB Tools
developer-guide/architecture/theme-syste.summary: Theme System DBTools.Presentation.dll holds every compiled WPF resource of the product: the theme dictionaries, stable controls and window shells. It stays loaded for the life of the Revit process. Tool views are raw XAML that Presentation parses at run time, so App, Core and the tool assemblies contain no BAML and no .g.resources. Each window merges the theme into its own resources, never into Application.Resources, so DB Tools does not change the appearance of other add-ins. Assembly roles Assembly Compiled WPF content DBTools.Presentation Theme dictionaries, stable windows and controls, tool behaviors, converters, controls and compiled settings views under Tools/<TOOL>/, and the merged Helix theme DBTools.HandyControl The HandyControl skins and themes DBTools.Core None. Window lifecycle, error boundaries, registry, commands and runtime hosts can be reloaded Tool assemblies None. Tool views and markup-only settings views are embedded as raw XAML Presentation lists its Page and EmbeddedResource items explicitly (EnableDefaultPageItems=false); default Compile inclusion picks up their code-behind. Tool assemblies contain no compiled WPF pages.
